newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: HAVEL LISTS DOUBTS ABOUT NEW ECON PLAN, CROWN FIRMS.
newsitem.headline: HAVEL LISTS DOUBTS ABOUT NEW ECON PLAN, CROWN FIRMS.

text.p: Czech President Vaclav Havel cast a pall over the ruling coalition's latest economic recovery programme on Thursday, saying he had doubts about its long-term aims and accompanying ministerial changes.

In a statement issued by his office, Havel said that while the programme agreed late on Wednesday could possibly resolve the immediate situation, it did not address what the government intended to do in the longer term.

Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus and his two junior coalition partners agreed to unspecified budget cuts, public sector wage freezes, and ministerial changes aimed at halting a crisis of confidence in the crown, the economy and the government.
Havel said that he expressed "several doubts" about the plan in a meeting with the three coalition leaders on Thursday, but indicated he might confirm the cabinet changes on Monday.
He said it "still does not mention even a word about long-term programme aims of this coalition and government, and does not, in the new situation, develop and make concrete its programme statement."
Havel said the plan did not offer "even a word" of who was responsible for the economic crisis, and that he could not understand the connection between the personnel changes and the new programme.

The agreement follows two weeks of speculative pressure on the Czech crown which culminated in the Czech National Bank (CNB) having to allow the currency the float, which sparked another eight percent drop in the currency.
The crown firmed against the mark in morning trade to stand at 19.138 to the mark and 32.575 to the dollar at 1130 GMT, compared with 19.306 and 32.737 late on Wednesday.
"The crown reacted positively to the changes in the government and the newly announced plan," said trader Jan Dosek of CSOB.

"Everything they want to do is great. I just give them about a five percent chance of actually being able to execute it and that is what the market is sceptical about," said Matt Starr, director of capital markets at Creditanstalt in Prague.

In a dramatic statement on Wednesday, Klaus, a forcefully confident monetarist economist who has taken personal the credit for the post-Communist economic transformation, admitted that mistakes were made during his five years in charge.
He said the recovery programme, which comes on top of another set of measures in April, would be painful but the fastest way to restore growth.
In the meantime, the price would be higher inflation, more unemployment, lower wages and a fall in output, he said.

Education Minister Ivan Pilip is to take over as Finance Minister and the current Czech ambassador to Britain Karel Kuhnl will be the new Trade and Industry Minister. Pilip, seen as part of Klaus's inner circle, replaces Ivan Kocarnik, blamed by many Czechs for the worsening economic situation.
